question: How do tracing, evaluations, and Signals fit together?
answer: I reached this turn's research limit without a draft passing all checks. Research may be incomplete, or the verifier may have rejected a useful draft; this does not establish that the docs lack an answer. Inspect the trace for the stopping reason.

candidate.answer:
**Short version:** tracing records what your system did, evaluations measure quality, and Signals score and tag agent activity that has already been traced. In the docs I read, Signals work on agent traces. The docs don't describe evaluations as feeding into Signals.

**1. Tracing records the data**
- Weave is described as an observability and evaluation platform [S2].
- It has two tracing approaches that produce separate traces, even in the same project [S4]:
  - *Agent tracing* is for agents and conversations. These traces appear on the **Agents** page.
  - *Application instrumentation* is for discrete calls such as a RAG pipeline. These `weave.op` calls appear on the **Traces** page.

**2. Signals score agent traces**
- Signals are tags and ratings shown in the Signals tab of the Agents view. They flag quality and safety problems and point you to the traces that need attention [S1].
- A *rating* is a numeric score from 0.0 to 1.0. *Tags* are labels, such as "user-frustration" or "nsfw", assigned to matching spans [S6].
- Signals are built for production monitoring of agent turns [S1]. A *turn* is one back-and-forth exchange between the user and the agent [S6].
- You can also score turns with an HTTP endpoint that you host instead of an LLM judge [S1].

**3. Evaluations are for benchmarking**
- Evaluations let you benchmark performance, track which model and prompt versions led to which results, define metrics with scoring functions, and compare evaluations [S7].

**How they connect**
1. Trace your agent. That gives Signals something to score.
2. Use Signals to watch production behavior and find problem conversations.
3. Use evaluations to measure changes to prompts or models in a structured, repeatable way.

**Caveat: legacy Monitors**
The "Monitor production" section of the overview says you can score production traffic with the same scorers you use in evaluation [S5]. That section links to the older Monitors page, which is a different workflow from the agent Signals described above. I haven't blended the two. I also didn't find a page in this snapshot that explains how evaluation scorers relate to agent Signals, so I can't say whether they are shared.

**Next step:** Start with agent tracing and look at your conversations in the Agents view. Then open the Signals tab to set up a signal.

# Monitor your agents with signals

> Use Weave signals to score agent turns, apply tags, and surface quality and safety issues in production.

> [!TIP]
>
> **This workflow is also available in CoreWeave Agent Lens.** Agent Lens is the Forge experience built for tracing, monitoring, and analyzing AI agents, with automated insights into agent failures and user intents. It uses the same trace data as Weights & Biases Weave, so the traces you already send appear there with nothing to migrate.
> [See how to do this in Agent Lens](https://docs.coreweave.com/products/agent-lens/tags/create-tag.md).

In Weave's [Agents view](https://docs.coreweave.com/products/wandb/weave/guides/tracking/view-agent-activity.md), the Signals tab shows tags and ratings for your agent's conversations. Signals surface quality and safety issues to flag problems, find patterns, and highlight the traces that need your attention. Use signals to automatically score the quality of your agent's responses, notice when a user is frustrated, or flag NSFW content.

To score turns with an HTTP endpoint that you host instead of an LLM judge, see [Score agent turns with a remote scorer](https://docs.coreweave.com/products/wandb/weave/guides/tracking/remote-scorer-signals.md).

all_read_evidence.heading: What is Weave?
all_read_evidence.text:
# What is Weave?

> Learn about W&B Weave and how it helps you build, evaluate, and improve LLM applications

W\&B Weave is an observability and evaluation platform for building reliable agents and LLM applications. Weave helps you understand what your AI application is doing, measure how well it performs, and systematically improve it over time.

Building LLM applications is fundamentally different from traditional software development. LLM outputs are non-deterministic, making debugging harder. Quality is subjective and context-dependent. Small prompt changes can cause unexpected behavior changes. Traditional testing approaches fall short.

# View agent activity

> Use Weave's Agents view to understand what your agent did, how much it cost, and exactly where things went right or wrong.

> [!TIP]
>
> **This workflow is also available in CoreWeave Agent Lens.** Agent Lens is the Forge experience built for tracing, monitoring, and analyzing AI agents, with automated insights into agent failures and user intents. It uses the same trace data as Weights & Biases Weave, so the traces you already send appear there with nothing to migrate.
> [See how to do this in Agent Lens](https://docs.coreweave.com/products/agent-lens/conversations/view-activity.md).

The Agents view gives you a turn-by-turn record of every conversation your agent had, along with token usage, tool invocations, and execution spans.

Agent applications are hard to debug because the interesting behavior happens between the user's request and the final response. The Agents view in Weave makes that middle layer visible. Every conversation your agent had is captured here, with the full message history, span-level execution detail, and token costs attached. You can see at a glance whether an agent completed its task, how many tool calls it made, and where time or budget was spent. For teams building and iterating on agents, this is the starting point for understanding behavior in production.

all_read_evidence.title: What is Weave?
all_read_evidence.heading: When to use agent tracing and when to use application instrumentation
all_read_evidence.text:
### When to use agent tracing and when to use application instrumentation

Choose which workflow to use based on what you want to observe:

* **Use agent tracing if you're building or running an agent.** This is the right fit if you use a supported agent harness or agent SDK, or if you've built a custom agent that you can instrument yourself.

* **Use application instrumentation if you're tracing application code.** This is the right fit for applications structured around discrete calls rather than conversations, such as a RAG pipeline, a summarization endpoint, or custom business logic.

Each approach records traces in its own part of the UI: agent traces appear on the **Agents** page, and `weave.op` calls appear on the **Traces** page. You can use both approaches in the same Weave project, but they produce separate traces.

If you're not sure where to start and your system involves an agent, start with agent tracing using the [agent integration quickstart](https://docs.coreweave.com/products/wandb/weave/agent-integration-quickstart.md). Otherwise, start with the [Op tracing quickstart](https://docs.coreweave.com/products/wandb/weave/quickstart.md).

## Evaluations

Benchmark and monitor your agent's or LLM application's performance with evaluations to iteratively improve quality and reliability.

* Track which model and prompt versions resulted in what performance.
* Define metrics to evaluate responses using one or more scoring functions.
* Compare two or more different evaluations over multiple metrics. Contrast specific samples for their performance.

[Build an evaluation pipeline](https://docs.coreweave.com/products/wandb/weave/tutorial-eval.md)

all_read_evidence.heading: Monitor using built-in signals
all_read_evidence.text:
# Monitor using built-in signals

> Weights & Biases provides built-in scoring solutions for agents in production

> [!NOTE]
>
> This page covers a previous approach to monitoring production traffic. For new implementations, use **Signals** under Weave for Agents. See [View agent signals](https://docs.coreweave.com/products/wandb/weave/guides/tracking/view-agent-signals.md).

Standard system metrics like latency, token count, and cost don't fully capture agent behavior. Inspecting individual traces provides deep insight but doesn't scale to the millions of traces generated in a live environment.

Signals provide a high-level monitoring solution to this problem by offering automated, behavioral scoring for agents in production:

* Automated scoring: Every incoming production trace is automatically processed and scored on common quality issues and errors.
* Infrastructure: Processing is powered by CoreWeave compute and CoreWeave GPUs for scalability across millions of traces.

By using signals within production, you can:

* Gain behavioral insight. Move beyond system metrics to understand if your agent is hallucinating, failing to follow conversation patterns, or losing grounding in its evidence.
* Accelerate the research loop. Use the scores and failure analyses generated by signals to identify weaknesses, which you can use to research model improvement, data annotation, or reinforcement learning.

results.title: View agent activity
results.heading: Get started
results.snippet:
## Get started

To open the Agents view for your project:

1. Navigate to [Forge](https://forge.coreweave.com/wandb) and select your project.
2. In the sidebar menu, select **Agents** to view all agent conversations saved for your project.

The Agents view is organized into a row of tabs across the top: **Dashboard**, **Agents**, **Conversations**, **Spans**, and **Signals**. The **Dashboard** tab gives a project-wide overview of agent activity, while the other tabs let you drill into individual agents, conversations, spans, and signals.

results.title: Monitor your agents with signals
results.heading: Manage and edit signals
results.snippet:
## Manage and edit signals

If you have at least one created signal, select the active signals button in the toolbar—labeled with the number of active signals, such as **1 active signals**—to open a drawer that lists all active signals for the project. From there you can toggle signals on or off, delete them, or edit any signal. The editor shows the same configuration fields as a custom signal.

results.title: Monitor using built-in signals
results.heading: Manage active signals
results.snippet:
## Manage active signals

After your signals are running, you can review which ones are active or turn off signals you no longer need. To view or remove active signals:

1. From the Monitors page, select the **Manage signals** () button. This opens a drawer listing all currently active signals grouped by category.
2. Hover over a signal and select the **Remove signal** () button to deactivate the signal.

Removing a signal stops scoring new traces. Weave preserves existing scores from the signal.

results.title: Monitor using built-in signals
results.heading: Available signals
results.snippet:
## Available signals

Weave offers monitors with built-in signals: preset scorers that evaluate production traces for common quality issues and errors by default, with no custom setup. Each built-in signal uses a benchmarked LLM prompt to classify traces and saves the results as comma-delimited tags representing the detected issues.

Signals use a [Serverless Inference](https://docs.coreweave.com/products/inference/serverless.md) model to score traces, so you don't need external API keys.

Weave provides 13 preset signals organized into two groups.

results.title: Trace sub-agents
results.heading: Sub-agent data model
results.snippet:
## Sub-agent data model

Before instrumenting your code, it helps to understand how Weave represents sub-agents in a trace. The `weave.start_subagent` span maps to the OTel `invoke_agent` span and emits the same operation name as the parent turn. Weave distinguishes the two by their parent-child relationship in the trace:

```plaintext theme={"system"}
Turn (invoke_agent — root span)
├── LLM call (chat)              ← parent agent's reasoning
│   └── SubAgent (invoke_agent)  ← delegation happens here
```

results.title: Send OpenTelemetry spans to the Agents view
results.heading: Shape spans for the Agents view
results.snippet:
## Shape spans for the Agents view

Weave accepts any OTel span and stores all of its attributes, but the Agents view renders spans that follow the [OTel GenAI semantic conventions](https://github.com/open-telemetry/semantic-conventions-genai/blob/main/docs/gen-ai/gen-ai-agent-spans.md). Set `gen_ai.operation.name` on each span to tell Weave what the span represents:

| `gen_ai.operation.name` | Represents | Rendered as |
| - | - | - |
| `invoke_agent` | One complete user-agent exchange. | A turn. |
| `chat` | One call to a language model API. | An LLM call within a turn. |
| `execute_tool` | One tool execution. | A tool call. |

Two more attributes control grouping:

* `gen_ai.conversation.id`: Groups turns into a conversation. Use a stable ID for the lifetime of the conversation.
* `gen_ai.agent.name`: Groups conversations under a named agent in the Agents tab.

Other GenAI semantic-convention attributes, such as `gen_ai.request.model`, `gen_ai.usage.input_tokens`, and `gen_ai.usage.output_tokens`, enrich the rendering with model names and token counts but are optional. For the age

# What is Weave?

> Learn about W&B Weave and how it helps you build, evaluate, and improve LLM applications

W\&B Weave is an observability and evaluation platform for building reliable agents and LLM applications. Weave helps you understand what your AI application is doing, measure how well it performs, and systematically improve it over time.

Building LLM applications is fundamentally different from traditional software development. LLM outputs are non-deterministic, making debugging harder. Quality is subjective and context-dependent. Small prompt changes can cause unexpected behavior changes. Traditional testing approaches fall short.

The Agents view gives you a turn-by-turn record of every conversation your agent had, along with token usage, tool invocations, and execution spans.

Agent applications are hard to debug because the interesting behavior happens between the user's request and the final response. The Agents view in Weave makes that middle layer visible. Every conversation your agent had is captured here, with the full message history, span-level execution detail, and token costs attached. For teams building and iterating on agents, this is the starting point for understanding behavior in production.

result.heading: When to use agent tracing and when to use application instrumentation
result.text:
### When to use agent tracing and when to use application instrumentation

Choose which workflow to use based on what you want to observe:

* **Use agent tracing if you're building or running an agent.** This is the right fit if you use a supported agent harness or agent SDK, or if you've built a custom agent that you can instrument yourself.

* **Use application instrumentation if you're tracing application code.** This is the right fit for applications structured around discrete calls rather than conversations, such as a RAG pipeline, a summarization endpoint, or custom business logic.

Each approach records traces in its own part of the UI: agent traces appear on the **Agents** page, and `weave.op` calls appear on the **Traces** page. You can use both approaches in the same Weave project, but they produce separate traces.

If you're not sure where to start and your system involves an agent, start with agent tracing using the [agent integration quickstart](https://docs.coreweave.com/products/wandb/weave/agent-integration-quickstart.md). Otherwise, start with the [Op tracing quickstart](https://docs.coreweave.com/products/wandb/weave/quickstart.md).

result.heading: Monitor using built-in signals
result.text:
# Monitor using built-in signals

> Weights & Biases provides built-in scoring solutions for agents in production

> [!NOTE]
>
> This page covers a previous approach to monitoring production traffic. For new implementations, use **Signals** under Weave for Agents. See [View agent signals](https://docs.coreweave.com/products/wandb/weave/guides/tracking/view-agent-signals.md).

Standard system metrics like latency, token count, and cost don't fully capture agent behavior. Inspecting individual traces provides deep insight but doesn't scale to the millions of traces generated in a live environment.

Signals provide a high-level monitoring solution to this problem by offering automated, behavioral scoring for agents in production:

* Automated scoring: Every incoming production trace is automatically processed and scored on common quality issues and errors.
* Infrastructure: Processing is powered by CoreWeave compute and CoreWeave GPUs for scalability across millions of traces.

By using signals within production, you can:

* Gain behavioral insight. Move beyond system metrics to understand if your agent is hallucinating, failing to follow conversation patterns, or losing grounding in its evidence.
* Accelerate the research loop. Use the scores and failure analyses generated by signals to identify weaknesses, which you can use to research model improvement, data annotation, or reinforcement learning.

Standard system metrics like latency, token count, and cost don't fully capture agent behavior. Inspecting individual traces provides deep insight but doesn't scale to the millions of traces generated in a live environment.

Signals provide a high-level monitoring solution to this problem by offering automated, behavioral scoring for agents in production:

* Automated scoring: Every incoming production trace is automatically processed and scored on common quality issues and errors.
* Infrastructure: Processing is powered by CoreWeave compute and CoreWeave GPUs for scalability across millions of traces.

By using signals within production, you can:

* Gain behavioral insight. Move beyond system metrics to understand if your agent is hallucinating, failing to follow conversation patterns, or losing grounding in its evidence.
* Accelerate the research loop. Use the scores and failure analyses generated by signals to identify weaknesses, which you can use to research model improvement, data annotation, or reinforcement learning.

## Get started

To view signals for your project:

1. Navigate to [Forge](https://forge.coreweave.com/wandb) and select your project.
2. In the sidebar menu, select **Agents** to view all agent conversations saved for your project.
3. In the tab bar, select **Signals**.

![The Signals tab showing a list of scored turns for the agent.](https://mintcdn.com/coreweave-dbfa0e8d/3Dv_sw2eg8feUJlx/products/wandb/weave/_media/agent-view-signals.png?fit=max\&auto=format\&n=3Dv_sw2eg8feUJlx\&q=85\&s=8c6cbeb0985f1892769e14cbf70fb16c)

# Monitor your agents with signals

> Use Weave signals to score agent turns, apply tags, and surface quality and safety issues in production.

> [!TIP]
>
> **This workflow is also available in CoreWeave Agent Lens.** Agent Lens is the Forge experience built for tracing, monitoring, and analyzing AI agents, with automated insights into agent failures and user intents. It uses the same trace data as Weights & Biases Weave, so the traces you already send appear there with nothing to migrate.
> [See how to do this in Agent Lens](https://docs.coreweave.com/products/agent-lens/tags/create-tag.md).

In Weave's [Agents view](https://docs.coreweave.com/products/wandb/weave/guides/tracking/view-agent-activity.md), the Signals tab shows tags and ratings for your agent's conversations. Signals surface quality and safety issues to flag problems, find patterns, and highlight the traces that need your attention. Use signals to automatically score the quality of your agent's responses, notice when a user is frustrated, or flag NSFW content.

To score turns with an HTTP endpoint that you host instead of an LLM judge, see [Score agent turns with a remote scorer](https://docs.coreweave.com/products/wandb/weave/guides/tracking/remote-scorer-signals.md).

input.answer:
**Short version:** tracing records what your system did. Evaluations benchmark performance. Signals add tags and ratings to your agent conversations to flag problems. The docs I read don't describe evaluations feeding into Signals.

**1. Tracing records the data**
- Weave is described as an observability and evaluation platform [S2].
- It has two tracing approaches that produce separate traces, even in the same project [S4].
- *Agent tracing* is for agents and conversations. These traces appear on the **Agents** page [S4].
- *Application instrumentation* is for discrete calls such as a RAG pipeline. These `weave.op` calls appear on the **Traces** page [S4].

**2. Signals sit in the Agents view**
- Signals are tags and ratings shown in the **Signals** tab of the Agents view. They flag quality and safety problems and point you to the traces that need attention [S1].
- To open the tab, select **Agents** in your project's sidebar, then select **Signals** [S9].
- A *rating* is a numeric score from 0.0 to 1.0. *Tags* are labels, such as "user-frustration" or "nsfw", assigned to matching spans. A *turn* is one back-and-forth exchange between the user and the agent [S6].
- You can also score turns with an HTTP endpoint that you host instead of an LLM judge [S1].

**3. Evaluations are for benchmarking**
- Evaluations let you benchmark performance, track which model and prompt versions led to which results, define metrics with scoring functions, and compare evaluations [S7].

**How they connect**
1. Agent tracing puts your conversations in the Agents view, and the Signals tab is part of that same view [S1][S3].
2. Signals help you find problem conversations in production [S1].
3. Evaluations are the separate place to measure and compare model and prompt changes [S7].

**Caveat: two different "Monitors/Signals" docs**
- The overview's "Monitor production" section says you can score production traffic with the same scorers you use in evaluation [S5]. It links to a Monitors page.
- That Monitors page says it covers a previous approach to monitoring production traffic. It says new implementations should use Signals under Weave for Agents [S8].
- I've kept the two separate. I found nothing in this snapshot that explains how evaluation scorers relate to agent Signals, so I can't say whether they are shared.

**Next step:** Open the **Signals** tab in your project's Agents view and see what is already scored. The "Create a new signal" section of the signals guide covers setup [S9].
